Most Angular developers learn dependency injection like this:

• Add @Injectable().

• Provide the service.

• Inject it into a component.

• Angular somehow finds it.
That explanation is enough — until something goes wrong.
You suddenly get:

• Two instances of a service that should have been shared

• Shared state between components that should have been isolated

• A provider that works in one route but fails elsewhere

• A NullInjectorError that appears to make no sense
The missing mental model is simple:
Angular does not search for dependencies globally. It walks an injector hierarchy and uses the nearest matching provider.
Dependency injection is a design pattern. But Angular’s implementation of that pattern behaves like a structured tree search.
Once you understand that tree, service scope, visibility, overrides, and lifetime become much easier to reason about.
A Token, a Provider, and an Instance
Whenever Angular injects something, three concepts are involved:

• Token: What is being requested

• Provider: Instructions for creating or retrieving it

• Instance: The value Angular eventually returns
For a service class, the class itself commonly acts as the token:
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class AuthService {
readonly isLoggedIn = signal(false);
}When another class requests AuthService, Angular looks through its injector hierarchy for a provider registered against the AuthService token.
@Component({
selector: 'app-header',
template: `...`
})
export class HeaderComponent {
private readonly auth = inject(AuthService);
}The important question is not merely:
“Was AuthService provided?”
The more useful question is:
“Which injector provided it, and which consumers can reach that injector?”
Angular Has Two Injector Hierarchies
In a standalone Angular application, dependency resolution mainly involves two related hierarchies:
1. ElementInjector
An ElementInjector is associated with elements in Angular’s component and directive tree.
It is normally empty unless a component or directive registers a provider through properties such as providers or viewProviders.
@Component({
selector: 'app-dashboard',
providers: [DashboardStateService],
template: `<app-widget />`
})
export class DashboardComponent {}Here, DashboardStateService belongs to the injector associated with that particular DashboardComponent instance.
Its descendants can access the service, but its parent and sibling branches cannot.
When another instance of DashboardComponent is created, Angular creates another locally scoped service instance. When the component is destroyed, its component-scoped service is destroyed with it.
2. EnvironmentInjector
The EnvironmentInjector hierarchy handles providers that are not tied directly to a particular component element.
This includes providers registered:

• At application bootstrap

• Through providedIn: ‘root’

• At route level using a route’s providers configuration
A route does not receive a separate EnvironmentInjector merely because it is lazy-loaded. Angular creates a route-specific EnvironmentInjector when that route declares providers.
For NgModule-based applications, Angular may also involve the ModuleInjector hierarchy.
How Angular Actually Resolves a Dependency
Suppose a widget requests DashboardStateService.
Angular resolves the token in two broad phases:

• It searches the current ElementInjector, then walks upward through parent element injectors.

• If the token is not found there, Angular delegates the request to the closest relevant EnvironmentInjector and continues upward through that hierarchy.
The first matching provider wins. A provider closer to the consumer shadows a provider registered farther away.
Consider this structure:
EnvironmentInjector hierarchyApplication EnvironmentInjector
│
└── Admin route EnvironmentInjector
└── Created because the route declares providers
ElementInjector hierarchyAppComponent
│
└── DashboardComponent
│ providers: [DashboardStateService]
│
└── WidgetComponent
requests DashboardStateServiceWhen WidgetComponent requests DashboardStateService, Angular:

• Checks the widget’s injector.

• Moves to the dashboard’s injector.

• Finds the provider.

• Returns that instance.

• Stops searching.
Angular never needs to reach the application-level environment injector for this token.
That “nearest provider wins” behaviour is what allows a component subtree to override an application-wide dependency without changing the rest of the application.
Root Scope and Component Scope Are Different Designs
These two provider configurations may use the same service class, but they create very different behaviour.
Root-scoped service
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class UserSessionService {
readonly currentUser = signal<User | null>(null);
}This is generally appropriate when you need:

• One shared instance

• Application-wide availability

• An application-length lifetime

• Tree-shakable automatic provisioning
Angular creates one shared root instance when the service is requested. Services configured through providedIn can also be removed from the production bundle when they are unused.
Component-scoped service
@Component({
selector: 'app-widget',
providers: [WidgetStateService],
template: `...`
})
export class WidgetComponent {
readonly state = inject(WidgetStateService);
}Every WidgetComponent instance receives its own WidgetStateService.
If the dashboard renders two widgets:
<app-widget />
<app-widget />the two widgets do not share state.
That is useful when the service represents:

• A form draft

• Modal state

• Widget configuration

• A temporary editing session

• Component-specific filters

• A short-lived workflow
A component provider is not simply a “smaller singleton.” It creates a separate instance for each instance of that component.
A Real Production Example
Imagine a configurable SaaS dashboard.
Every widget has:

• Its own filters

• Loading state

• Resize information

• Temporary edits

• Error state
A root-scoped service would cause every widget to share the same state:
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class WidgetStateService {
readonly loading = signal(false);
readonly filters = signal<Record<string, string>>({});
}That could produce bugs where changing one widget unexpectedly affects another.
Instead, scope the service to the widget:
@Injectable()
export class WidgetStateService {
readonly loading = signal(false);
readonly filters = signal<Record<string, string>>({});
}@Component({
selector: 'app-widget',
providers: [WidgetStateService],
template: `...`
})
export class WidgetComponent {
readonly state = inject(WidgetStateService);
}Now each widget owns an isolated instance.
The service’s scope reflects the scope of the state it manages.
That is the real design decision behind provider placement.
Injection Tokens Are Useful When a Class Cannot Be the Token
Not every dependency is a service class.
You may need to inject:

• An API URL

• Feature flags

• A configuration object

• A function

• An interface

• A browser-specific implementation
TypeScript interfaces disappear at runtime, so Angular cannot use them directly as runtime tokens.
Use an InjectionToken instead:
export interface ApiConfig {
baseUrl: string;
retryCount: number;
}export const API_CONFIG = new InjectionToken<ApiConfig>('API_CONFIG');Register a provider:
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, {
providers: [
{
provide: API_CONFIG,
useValue: {
baseUrl: 'https://api.example.com',
retryCount: 3
}
}
]
});Then inject it:
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class ApiService {
private readonly config = inject(API_CONFIG); getBaseUrl(): string {
return this.config.baseUrl;
}
}The token’s description is only useful for debugging. Two separately created InjectionToken objects remain different tokens, even when they use the same description.
Changing the Search with Injection Options
Angular lets you modify where dependency resolution starts and stops.
Modern inject()-based code can use options directly:
const logger = inject(LoggerService, {
optional: true
});const parentCache = inject(CacheService, {
skipSelf: true,
optional: true
});const localConfig = inject(ConfigService, {
self: true,
optional: true
});const hostState = inject(HostStateService, {
host: true,
optional: true
});These options mean:

• optional: Return null instead of throwing when no provider is found

• skipSelf: Start searching from the parent injector

• self: Search only the current injector

• host: Stop when the host component boundary is reached
They do not change the requested token. They change the boundaries of the search.
Also remember that inject() must execute inside an injection context, such as a field initializer, constructor, provider factory, functional guard, or a function explicitly executed through runInInjectionContext. Calling it later inside a normal component method or lifecycle hook results in an error.
Route-Scoped Providers
Route providers are useful when a service belongs to one feature rather than the entire application.
export const routes: Routes = [
{
path: 'admin',
providers: [
AdminStateService,
AdminPermissionsService
],
loadComponent: () =>
import('./admin/admin-page')
.then(module => module.AdminPage)
}
];Angular creates an EnvironmentInjector for this route and makes its providers available to the route and its descendants.
Components outside the route cannot access those providers because dependency resolution only walks upward through reachable injector ancestors — it does not search sideways into another route branch.
One lifecycle detail is easy to miss: route-scoped injectors are not necessarily destroyed as soon as the user navigates away. Current Angular documentation states that route injectors persist by default unless route-injector cleanup behaviour is explicitly enabled and configured. Do not use route scope as an automatic short-lived cleanup mechanism without checking your router configuration.
Common Dependency Injection Mistakes
Providing a shared service at component level
@Component({
providers: [UserSessionService]
})This creates a new session service for every component instance instead of using the shared application instance.
Putting temporary state in a root service
A root singleton can accidentally preserve state between components, routes, dialogs, or workflow instances.
Expecting a parent to access a child provider
Angular searches upward, not downward. A service provided by a child component cannot be injected by its parent.
Assuming lazy loading automatically defines service scope
Lazy loading controls when code is loaded. Provider placement controls service scope. They are related, but they are not the same concept.
Using self or skipSelf without drawing the hierarchy
Before using resolution modifiers, identify:

• The requesting element

• The current injector

• The parent injector

• The host boundary

• The environment injector involved
Otherwise, the modifier may produce the opposite of what you intended.
Under the Hood
Angular’s compiler generates factory information that the dependency injection system uses to instantiate injectable classes.
You may see private Ivy fields such as ɵfac and ɵprov in compiled output. They help explain how Angular represents factories and provider metadata, but they are internal implementation details and should not be referenced by application code.
The practical lesson is more important than the private field names:
Angular already knows how to construct the dependency because provider and factory information was generated or registered before the injection request occurred.
The injector’s job is to find the correct provider in the hierarchy and use it to obtain the value.
Interview Question
Two sibling components both declare the same service in their own providers arrays.
Do they share an instance?
No.
